title: Coena Domini: Brethren's hypotheses for the literal sense
pass_a_gloss: HYPOTHESES of the brother-men, which it has sufficed to recount here, weighed at length by Theologians, were e.g.: That a figurative sense overturns the truth of the words; That 'is Body' necessarily hints it is real, substantial; That Christ in the first Supper was bodily present — Therefore also in Bread & Wine, though that Christ was outside the Bread — Therefore bodily present after ascension into the Heavens; That Christ's Body is eaten in the Supper — therefore as present ἀδιαστάτως, nor can the Body be present in a spiritual mode; That sacramental eating says more than spiritual — therefore says oral eating of the true & natural Body; That it is safer to cling to the literal sense, from which the Reformed withdraw, and rashly; That what was instituted by these words is a Testament or Covenant — Therefore in proper words, because these alone are clear — as if a sign of the Covenant or Testament were not instituted, as we from Matt. 26:28; Luke 22:20. Thus they suppose τὸ κρινόμενον, namely that the Institution words (This is my Body) are explained by themselves in a literal, native, proper, perspicuous sense, while they so render: In or under this, namely the composed complex (of Bread & Body), is contained my Body — this very Body which is present to you, but illocal, &c.
pass_b_english: Our brethren’s hypotheses — enough to list them here; theologians have weighed them at length — include claims such as these: a figurative sense destroys the truth of the words; "is Body" must mean something real and substantial; Christ was bodily present at the first Supper, and therefore also in the bread and wine even while he stood outside the bread, and therefore remains bodily present after the ascension into the heavens; Christ’s Body is eaten in the Supper and so must be present without spatial distance, since a body cannot be present in a spiritual mode; sacramental eating means more than spiritual eating and therefore means oral eating of the true and natural Body; clinging to the literal sense is safer, and the Reformed leave it rashly; what these words institute is a Testament or Covenant and therefore must use proper words alone, as if clarity belonged only to proper speech — as though no sign of the Covenant or Testament were instituted, which is how we read Matthew 26:28 and Luke 22:20.

In that way they beg the question under judgment. They treat the Institution words ("This is my Body") as self-explanatory in a literal, native, proper, and clear sense, yet they paraphrase them as: in or under this — namely the composed complex of bread and Body — my Body is contained, this very Body present to you, yet illocal, and so forth.
source_text: HYPOTHESES Virorum fratrum, quas enarrasse hoc loco suffecerit, prolixe a Theologis expensas, fuere, ex. gr. Sensum figuratum evertere scilicet veritatem verborum: Illud, est Corpus, necessario innuere esse reale, substantiale: Christum in prima Coena fuisse corporaliter praesentem, Ergo & in Pane & Vino, qui tamen Christus erat extra Panem; Ergo corporaliter praesentem post ascens. in Caelos: Corpus Christi manducari in Coena, ergo ut ἀδιαστάτως praesens, nec Corpus posse esse praesens spirituali modo: Manducationem sacramentalem plus dicere quam spiritualem; E. dicere manducat. oralem Corporis veri & naturalis: Tutius esse adhaerere sensui literali, a quo scil. recedant Reformati, & temere quidem: Institutum quoque his verbis Testamentum, vel Pactum, Ergo verbis propriis, quia haec sola clara sint; quasi non institutum signum Foederis vel Testamenti, ut nos ex Matth. XXVI. 28. Luc. XXII. 20. Ita supponunt τὸ κρινόμενον, nempe explicari a se verba Institutionis (Hoc est Corpus meum) in sensu literali, nativo, proprio, perspicuo, dum ita reddunt: In vel sub hoc, scil. composito, complexo (Panis & Corporis) continetur Corpus meum, hoc ipsum Corpus quod vobis adest, sed illocale, &c.
